title: Wrestling at the river (Genesis 32:23–33)
hookLine: Jacob wrestles until dawn and is renamed Israel, one who strives with God

lines: ESAU IS COMING, WITH FOUR HUNDRED MEN.
cards: Esau is coming, with four hundred men. Free of Laban, Jacob is walking straight toward the other person he never settled with: the brother whose blessing he took before he ran.
When the scouts bring the news, Jacob splits his camp in two, so if one half is attacked the other can run. He sends gifts ahead, herd after herd.
At night, he sends his wives and children across the river Jabbok, with everything he owns. "And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day."
No warning, no name: a fight in the dark that lasts all night.

teach.h: I WILL NOT LET THEE GO.
teach.b: The stranger can't win, so he touches the hollow of Jacob's thigh and puts it out of joint. It's getting light, and he says, let me go. Jacob, hurt, holding on, answers: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."
The stranger asks a strange question. What's your name? Jacob.
That name carried: the heel-grabber, who came out holding his brother's heel and grabbed a blessing that wasn't his.

teach.h: YISRAEL: ONE WHO STRIVES WITH GOD.
teach.b: Then: "Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel; for thou hast striven with God and with men, and hast prevailed." Yisrael.
The first part comes from a Hebrew root meaning to strive, to struggle; the last, el, is God: one who strives with God. Who was the man? The text only says a man.

The prophet Hosea calls him an angel. A midrash says he was Esau's own angel, which makes the fight a rehearsal for tomorrow. Jacob names the place Peniel, saying he has seen God face to face and lived.
The Torah leaves it open, and the rabbis offer more than one answer.
Then the sun rises, and Jacob limps. The blessing doesn't erase the wound; he carries both. The Torah says that's why the children of Israel, to this day, don't eat the sinew of the thigh-vein.
And this became the name of a whole people. Not the ones who never doubted, or never argued. The ones who hold on in the dark and won't let go without a blessing.

teach.h: THOU HAST STRIVEN WITH GOD AND WITH MEN.
teach.b: Struggling with God isn't a failure of faith in this story. It's the name.

how: Observant Jews keep the Torah's rule not to eat the sciatic nerve, the gid hanasheh, which Genesis 32:33 ties to Jacob's limp; some readers also hear in the name Israel a permission to question and argue with God.

games.q: who's who at the river — tap the pairs.

s: the text says clearly that the wrestler was an angel
Genesis only says "a man." Hosea calls him an angel; a midrash says Esau's angel. the Torah leaves it open.
Jacob asks for a blessing before he lets go
"I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."
Jacob walks away from the fight unhurt
he limps at sunrise. the blessing doesn't erase the wound.

games.q: you're Jacob. you've wrestled all night, your hip is out of joint, and the stranger says: let me go, the day is breaking. what do you do?
o: let go. you're hurt and it's over.
hold on until he blesses you.
ask him to fight again tomorrow night.
games.why: he won't let go without a blessing, and the blessing turns out to be a new name: Israel, one who strives with God.

practice: Name one thing you're wrestling with right now: a question about God, if you have one, a decision, a person, something in yourself.

You don't have to win it; just name it plainly, the way the stranger asked Jacob his name, and notice you're still holding on. If you pray, you can bring the struggle with you; if not, just stay with it honestly.

wordCard.voice: Yisrael, Israel: one who strives with God and with people, and holds on.
